Lightning and thunder basics (charge separation; shock wave from rapid heating)

Tropical cyclone formation over warm ocean water

claims.claim: All thunderstorms require three ingredients for formation: moisture, instability, and a lifting mechanism.

Air is unstable when it keeps rising after being nudged upward; an unstable air mass has warm, moist air near the surface and cold, dry air aloft, so a rising parcel cools, its water vapor condenses, and a tall cumulonimbus cloud grows.

Lightning results from the separation of electric charge inside a thunderstorm, leaving a negatively charged base and a positively charged top; collisions involving ice, hail, and semi-frozen droplets (graupel) are essential to the process, and storms that produce little ice usually produce little lightning. Exactly how lightning forms has not been fully verified, so this is the leading theoretical account.
Thunder is the acoustic shock wave produced when lightning heats the air along its channel to about 54,000°F (30,000°C) in a fraction of a second, causing explosive expansion of the air.

A tornado is a violently rotating column of air descending from a thunderstorm and in contact with the ground; most destructive tornadoes are spawned by supercell thunderstorms (storms with a persistent rotating updraft, or mesocyclone), and strong vertical wind shear — changes in wind speed and/or direction with height — is the environment most supportive of supercells. The exact processes that form the funnel are not fully known.

The Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale rates tornadoes by the damage they cause and estimates wind speeds from that damage; the categories are EF0 (65-85 mph), EF1 (86-110 mph), EF2 (111-135 mph), EF3 (136-165 mph), EF4 (166-200 mph), and EF5 (greater than 200 mph, open-ended). The National Weather Service implemented the EF scale in 2007, replacing the original Fujita scale.

Tropical cyclones are warm-core low-pressure systems with organized circulation that form over tropical or subtropical waters; favorable conditions include ocean water of at least about 80°F (27°C) through a depth of roughly 150 feet, an atmosphere unstable to moist convection, moist mid-level air, a pre-existing near-surface disturbance, low vertical wind shear (less than about 23 mph), and a location far enough from the equator (generally at least 300 miles) for the Coriolis effect to spin the system up.

Warm ocean water powers tropical cyclones: condensing water vapor releases heat that warms the air and keeps it rising, drawing in more surface air as wind; once the center moves over land, the storm weakens because it is cut off from the ocean's moisture and heat.

The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale is a 1-5 rating of a hurricane's present intensity based only on maximum sustained wind speed: Category 1 (74-95 mph), Category 2 (96-110 mph), Category 3 (111-129 mph), Category 4 (130-156 mph), and Category 5 (157 mph or higher); it does not consider storm surge, rainfall-induced flooding, or tornadoes.

The same type of storm carries different names by basin: hurricane in the North Atlantic and Northeast Pacific, typhoon in the Northwest Pacific, and tropical cyclone (or regional variants such as severe cyclonic storm) elsewhere.

Tropical storms and hurricanes are given short, distinctive names from lists agreed upon internationally through the World Meteorological Organization; the Atlantic lists are six rotating sets reused on a six-year cycle, names draw from many languages, and the names of deadly or highly destructive storms are retired and replaced.

A blizzard is defined by the National Weather Service as sustained winds or frequent gusts of 35 mph or greater with considerable falling and/or blowing snow reducing visibility frequently to less than one-quarter mile, with these conditions expected to prevail for three hours or longer.

A watch means the conditions are favorable for severe weather in and close to the watch area, but the occurrence is neither certain nor imminent, and a watch is not a warning; a warning means the hazardous weather is occurring, imminent, or highly likely — for example, a severe thunderstorm warning is issued when a severe thunderstorm is indicated by radar or reported by a spotter — and warnings are issued by local National Weather Service offices for a short window.
A thunderstorm is classified severe by the National Weather Service when it produces hail one inch or larger in diameter and/or winds of 58 mph or greater.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How lightning forms is not fully verified.
positions: JetStream: 'exactly how lightning forms has never been verified, so there is room for debate'; leading theories center on separation of electric charge and generation of an electric field, with ice, hail, and semi-frozen drops essential.
Some popular accounts describe lightning simplistically as static-electricity buildup with no caveat about uncertainty.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents charge separation and field generation as the leading theoretical account and notes the uncertainty explicitly; no claim of fully confirmed mechanics is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Tornado formation is not completely understood.
positions: JetStream: 'the exact processes for the formation of a funnel are not known yet'; supercells in strong vertical wind shear are the favored environment.
NSSL: 'the truth is that we don't fully understand' tornado formation; mesocyclone-scale processes are believed to dictate it.
Older textbook treatments sometimes present a single fixed formation sequence.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the well-established conditions (supercells, wind shear, mesocyclones) as the favored environment and explicitly notes that the exact funnel-forming processes remain an open research question.

conflictingEvidence.issue: EF scale wind estimates versus measured winds.
positions: SPC: EF winds are estimated from structural and/or tree damage; the original F-scale wind estimates were judged too high (e.g., for the 1997 Jarrell and 1999 Moore tornadoes).
NSSL: EF ratings are assigned by examining damage, with 28 damage indicators and 8 degrees of damage each; EF5 ratings are open-ended because of uncertainty in the strongest winds.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson consistently describes the EF scale as damage-based with estimated wind speeds, uses the JetStream/SPC category ranges, and notes that EF5 has no upper bound.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Saffir-Simpson category is often mistaken for overall hurricane danger.
positions: JetStream classification page: the scale 'only addresses the wind speed and does not consider the potential for other hurricane-related impacts, such as storm surge, rainfall-induced floods, and tornadoes.'
Common usage treats higher category as automatically meaning greater total hazard in all respects.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states plainly that Saffir-Simpson measures maximum sustained wind only and that surge, rainfall flooding, and tornadoes are separate hazards.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft described storms as a general 'foundational concept' ('a label on a toolbox drawer', 'building block for later discussions') with no severe-weather content; all of that boilerplate was discarded as unsupported by any source.
The draft's definitions of vocabulary ('context', 'evidence', 'application') are generic and were replaced with storm-specific terms.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire boilerplate draft with verified severe-weather science: thunderstorm ingredients, lightning/thunder basics, tornado conditions, tropical cyclone formation, and blizzard criteria.
Added the Enhanced Fujita scale wind ranges (EF0-EF5) from NOAA JetStream, cross-checked against the SPC EF-scale page (EF3 = 136-165 mph appears in both).
Added the Saffir-Simpson wind-speed categories (74-95, 96-110, 111-129, 130-156, 157+ mph) from NOAA JetStream and emphasized that the scale is wind-only.
Added the factual watch-versus-warning distinction (possible-but-uncertain versus occurring/imminent) from the NWS glossary and JetStream.
Added the NWS blizzard definition (35 mph winds, one-quarter-mile visibility, three hours).
Added the NWS severe-thunderstorm definition (1-inch hail and/or 58 mph winds) as supporting context.
Framed all safety references in general preparedness terms (the value of warnings) with no individualized safety advice.
rightsIssues: All sources are U.S. government publications (NOAA, NWS, SPC, NSSL); registered as REFERENCE_ONLY and used for facts only, with all prose synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: JetStream: Ingredients for a Thunderstorm
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service JetStream (Online School for Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: the three required thunderstorm ingredients (moisture, instability, and a lifting mechanism); unstable air as air that continues rising when nudged, characterized by warm moist air near the surface and cold dry air aloft; the rising parcel cooling and condensing to form cumulonimbus; sources of lift including differential heating, fronts, dry lines, outflow boundaries, and terrain. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: JetStream: How Lightning is Created
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service JetStream (Online School for Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: lightning formation never fully verified; leading theories of charge separation and electric field generation within the storm; ice, hail, and semi-frozen droplets essential to lightning development; storms failing to produce large quantities of ice usually failing to produce lightning; negatively charged cloud base and positively charged top; forecasting when and where lightning will strike not yet possible. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: JetStream: The Sound of Thunder
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service JetStream (Online School for Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: thunder as the acoustic shock wave resulting from the extreme heat generated by a lightning flash; lightning as hot as 54,000°F (30,000°C), about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun; explosive expansion of air heated in a fraction of a second compressing air ahead of it into a shock wave similar to a sonic boom. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: JetStream: Thunderstorm Hazards - Tornadoes
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service JetStream (Online School for Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: tornado definition (violently rotating, usually counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, column of air descending from a thunderstorm in contact with the ground); about 1,200 tornadoes per year in the United States with an April-June peak concentrated in the central U.S.; most tornadoes spawned by supercells with persistent rotating updrafts in environments of strong vertical wind shear; wind shear as change in wind speed and/or direction with height; mesocyclone formation; the EF-scale table with wind speeds EF0 65-85, EF1 86-110, EF2 111-135, EF3 136-165, EF4 166-200, EF5 greater than 200 mph (open-ended); the exact processes of funnel formation not yet known; even EF5 tornadoes do not reduce air pressure enough to cause a house to explode. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: JetStream: Staying Ahead of the Storms
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service JetStream (Online School for Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: convective outlooks as SPC risk forecasts; watches issued when conditions become favorable for severe thunderstorms and tornadoes, covering large areas (about 20,000-40,000 square miles) for roughly four to six hours; 'a watch is NOT a warning' and is not a guarantee of severe weather; warnings issued by local NWS Weather Forecast Offices. Used for the general watch-versus-warning framing; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: JetStream: Tropical Cyclone Introduction
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service JetStream (Online School for Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: tropical cyclone as a warm-core low-pressure system without fronts developing over tropical or subtropical waters with organized circulation; favorable conditions including warm ocean waters of at least 80°F (27°C) through a depth of about 150 feet, an atmosphere cooling fast enough with height to be potentially unstable to moist convection, relatively moist mid-tropospheric air, a pre-existing near-surface disturbance, low vertical wind shear (less than about 23 mph), and a minimum distance of about 300 miles from the equator; warm water as the most important factor powering the storm through condensation heat release; rapid weakening after the center moves over land because the storm loses the ocean's moisture and heat; Atlantic hurricane season June 1-November 30 with peak activity in early to mid September. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: JetStream: Tropical Cyclone Classification
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service JetStream (Online School for Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale as a 1-5 rating based on the hurricane's present intensity that only addresses wind speed and does not consider storm surge, rainfall-induced floods, or tornadoes; category wind speeds Category 1 (74-95 mph), Category 2 (96-110 mph), Category 3 (111-129 mph), Category 4 (130-156 mph), Category 5 (157 mph or greater); regional names (hurricane in the North Atlantic/Northeast Pacific, typhoon in the Northwest Pacific, severe tropical cyclone/severe cyclonic storm in other basins). Table values verified against the source text. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: JetStream: Tropical Cyclone Names
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service JetStream (Online School for Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: short distinctive given names being quicker and less error-prone than latitude-longitude identifiers; names reducing confusion when two or more tropical storms occur at the same time; name lists drawing from a variety of languages because hurricanes affect multiple nations; lists agreed upon at international meetings of the World Meteorological Organization; the National Hurricane Center assigning names from six rotating Atlantic lists (one set per year, reused after all six are used); names of deadly or destructive storms retired; letters Q, U, X, Y, and Z excluded from the lists. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: National Weather Service Glossary: Blizzard
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports the blizzard definition: sustained wind or frequent gusts to 35 mph or greater, with considerable falling and/or blowing snow reducing visibility frequently to less than one-quarter mile, conditions expected to prevail for 3 hours or longer; also the Blizzard Warning entry (same criteria, expected to prevail for a minimum of 3 hours). No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: National Weather Service Glossary: Watch
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports the watch concept: e.g., Flash Flood Watch issued when conditions are favorable for the hazard in and close to the watch area but the occurrence is neither certain nor imminent; Severe Thunderstorm Watch issued when conditions are favorable for the development of severe thunderstorms in and close to the watch area, normally issued well in advance of the actual occurrence. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: National Weather Service Glossary: Warning
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports the warning concept: hazards occurring, imminent, or highly likely (e.g., Coastal/Lakeshore Flood Warning); Severe Thunderstorm Warning issued when a severe thunderstorm is indicated by WSR-88D radar or reported by a spotter (hail 1 inch or larger and/or winds equal or exceeding 58 mph), issued by the local National Weather Service Forecast Office, usually for about one hour; Tornado Warning issued when a tornado is indicated by radar or sighted by spotters, issued by the local office, usually about 30 minutes, and can be issued without a prior watch. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Enhanced Fujita Scale (EF Scale)
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: Fujita's 1971 introduction of the F-scale; F-scale winds estimated from structural and/or tree damage; the revision prompted by the 1997 Jarrell and 1999 Moore/Oklahoma City tornadoes (FEMA 342 building assessment); the worked example rating a damaged brick-veneer home EF-3 with winds between 136-165 mph (cross-check for the EF3 range); the EF scale's damage-based method. The EF category wind table on this page is an image; the EF ranges were taken from the JetStream tornadoes page text and cross-checked against this page's EF3 statement. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Severe Weather 101: Tornado Basics
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA NSSL). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: tornado as a narrow, violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground; tornado strength rated by examining damage and estimating wind speeds; the Enhanced Fujita scale implemented by the National Weather Service in 2007 with 28 damage indicators and 8 degrees of damage each; the statement that 'the truth is that we don't fully understand' tornado formation, with the most destructive tornadoes occurring from supercells with mesocyclones; EF5 ratings open-ended (greater than 200 mph). Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.
